name: Greenspan's 1% and the 2005 'no bubble' speech
scope: The late Greenspan years and the interest-rate policy that fueled the housing bubble. T1: ALAN GREENSPAN, Fed chair from August 11 1987 through January 31 2006, was the longest-serving Fed chairman in modern history. T2: after the dot-com crash of 2000-01, Greenspan's Fed cut the FEDERAL FUNDS RATE from 6.5% in December 2000 down to 1.0% by JUNE 2003 -- and HELD it at 1% for a full year, the lowest rates in 46 years at the time. T3: those artificially cheap rates poured cash into the housing market. Home prices, which had risen at roughly the rate of inflation for decades, began rising 10-15% per year in coastal markets. Mortgage originators like Countrywide and Ameriquest, freed by low rates and Fannie/Freddie loan-purchase demand, wrote enormous volumes of subprime loans (no-doc 'liar loans', 2/28 ARMs, negative-amortization mortgages). T4: on OCTOBER 27 2005, at an American Bankers Association conference, Greenspan gave a speech dismissing housing-bubble concerns. He acknowledged 'froth' in some local markets but argued that a national bubble was implausible because housing was a heterogeneous local market (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact date and wording of Greenspan's 2005 ABA remarks). Two years later the national housing market entered the collapse that triggered the Global Financial Crisis. T5: Austrian analysts (Peter Schiff on CNBC 2005-07, Ron Paul in Congress, Mark Thornton at the Mises Institute) had been publicly warning since 2003 that the low-rate policy was creating an unsustainable housing boom -- classic ABCT: artificially low interest rates cause CAPITAL to be misallocated into interest-sensitive sectors (housing, long-duration assets); the bust is inevitable because the underlying savings to sustain the malinvestment do not exist. Greenspan's post-crisis 2008 congressional testimony admitted he had found 'a flaw' in his worldview. Further rungs: Greenspan's DOCTORATE thesis at NYU (2007) was later reported to include a chapter on housing prices; his 1966 essay 'Gold and Economic Freedom' argued for a gold standard -- a position he abandoned when he took the Fed chair; his memoir 'The Age of Turbulence' (2007) sold 1M+ copies just as the bubble he helped create was breaking.

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a Fed chairman told bankers in 2005 there was NO national housing bubble, and two years later everything collapsed) and T5 (Austrian analysts on cable news were warning about the exact bust that came, and were laughed at). The SEEN was cheap mortgages and rising home values; the UNSEEN was the malinvestment being built into interest-sensitive sectors that would collapse when rates rose. name: The 2004-06 rate hikes and the inverted yield curve
scope: The tightening cycle that popped the housing bubble and rang the classic recession warning bell. T1: after holding the federal funds rate at 1% for a year, the Fed began raising rates on JUNE 30 2004 -- Greenspan's first hike in four years, a quarter-point (25 basis points) to 1.25%. T2: over the next TWO YEARS the Fed raised rates SEVENTEEN CONSECUTIVE TIMES, each hike exactly 25bp, taking the fed funds rate from 1.00% to 5.25% by JUNE 29 2006 -- the last hike of Greenspan's era, executed by his successor Ben Bernanke who had taken the chair February 1 2006. T3: adjustable-rate mortgages written at 2003-04 teaser rates began RESETTING in 2006-07 to the new higher rates, doubling or tripling many households' monthly payments overnight. Subprime foreclosure notices began climbing in the second half of 2006; the ABX subprime-index started falling in early 2007. T4: by late 2006 the YIELD CURVE was INVERTED -- short-term Treasury yields (2-year) were HIGHER than long-term yields (10-year). Since Estrella and Mishkin's 1996 New York Fed research paper, an inverted yield curve for a full quarter had been the single most reliable recession predictor in the US data, correctly signaling every recession since 1968. T5: the inversion held through most of 2007. The recession began in December 2007 (NBER dating); Bear Stearns's hedge funds collapsed July-August 2007; Lehman failed September 15 2008. The Fed's own recession-warning tool had rung the bell for TWO YEARS before the crisis arrived -- and the Fed kept telling markets the housing problems were 'contained.' Further rungs: the phrase 'measured pace' (the FOMC's coded language for '25bp per meeting') became a market cliche in 2004-06; former FDIC chair Sheila Bair later called this cycle 'the most predictable financial crisis in American history.'

name: Helicopter Ben: Bernanke's 2002 deflation speech
scope: The speech that gave Ben Bernanke his nickname and previewed his crisis toolkit. T1: BEN BERNANKE, then a Fed governor (he became chairman on February 1 2006), gave a speech on NOVEMBER 21 2002 to the National Economists Club in Washington titled 'DEFLATION: MAKING SURE IT DOESN'T HAPPEN HERE.' T2: the speech argued that a central bank with a FIAT (non-gold-backed) currency ALWAYS has the tools to fight deflation because it can create money at zero marginal cost. Bernanke invoked MILTON FRIEDMAN's famous thought experiment -- if deflation ever became a real threat, the central bank could in theory 'drop money from a helicopter.' T3: Bernanke listed CONCRETE UNCONVENTIONAL TOOLS the Fed could use once short-term rates hit zero: BUY LONG-TERM TREASURIES to lower long-term yields, buy AGENCY debt, buy FOREIGN government bonds, and (in extreme cases) fund direct tax cuts by printing money. Nearly every one of these tools was deployed in 2008-14 as QE1, QE2, Operation Twist, and QE3. T4: the media nickname 'HELICOPTER BEN' stuck to him for the rest of his career. It was originally a Friedman metaphor -- Friedman used it in his 1969 essay 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' as a pedagogical device, NOT as policy advocacy -- but Bernanke's citation turned it into a proposed toolkit. Austrian economists (Bob Murphy, Peter Schiff, Jim Rogers) immediately criticized the 2002 speech as a blueprint for eventual currency debasement. T5: exactly SIX YEARS after the speech (November 2008), Bernanke -- now Fed chair -- launched QE1, buying $600B of mortgage-backed securities and $300B of Treasuries. The 2002 speech was, in retrospect, the most accurate PREVIEW of Fed crisis policy ever given: everything Bernanke said the Fed COULD do, he ended up doing. Further rungs: the 2002 speech also included the famous concession that if 'necessary,' the Fed could always fund tax cuts by monetization -- what critics called 'monetary financing of fiscal policy'; Bernanke's academic specialty had been the Great Depression, and he cited Friedman + Schwartz 1963 throughout the speech.

name: 'You're right, we did it': Bernanke's Friedman apology
scope: The Fed's public admission that it caused the Great Depression. T1: on NOVEMBER 8 2002, at a conference honoring MILTON FRIEDMAN'S 90TH BIRTHDAY at the University of Chicago, then-Fed-governor BEN BERNANKE gave a speech. T2: Friedman and Anna Schwartz, in their 1963 'A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960,' had argued that the Fed CAUSED the Great Depression by allowing the money supply to CONTRACT roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933 -- letting bank failures cascade instead of acting as lender of last resort. It was the central thesis of one of the most important economics books of the 20th century. T3: for decades, mainstream economists had resisted the Friedman-Schwartz thesis, preferring Keynesian aggregate-demand explanations. Bernanke, an academic historian of the Depression himself, closed his 2002 speech with an EXTRAORDINARY concession delivered directly to the 90-year-old Friedman in the audience. T4: the words: 'Let me end my talk by abusing slightly my status as an official representative of the Federal Reserve. I would like to say to MILTON and ANNA: Regarding the Great Depression. YOU'RE RIGHT, WE DID IT. WE'RE VERY SORRY. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording from the Fed archive; Bernanke's speech remains on federalreserve.gov.) T5: this is one of the most remarkable admissions ever made by a central bank -- an official Fed representative, in public, at a birthday party, acknowledging that his institution CAUSED the worst economic catastrophe in modern American history. And yet six years later, the SAME chairman who apologized for the 1929-33 contraction presided over policies (2008-14 QE, ZIRP) that his Austrian critics argue caused a NEW mispricing of capital and the 2020-24 inflation wave. Further rungs: Friedman died November 16 2006 at age 94, before he could see the full 2008 Fed response; Anna Schwartz lived until 2012, and in a 2008 Wall Street Journal interview she sharply criticized Bernanke, saying 'he has no true understanding of what is going on' -- reversing the endorsement Bernanke had claimed six years earlier.

name: Bear Stearns and the $2 share weekend rescue
scope: The first modern investment-bank rescue and the moral-hazard opening act of the Global Financial Crisis. T1: BEAR STEARNS, founded 1923, was the FIFTH-LARGEST US investment bank in 2007 with major exposure to subprime mortgages and mortgage-backed securities. Its two internal hedge funds had already collapsed in July-August 2007. T2: through the week of MARCH 10-14 2008, Bear's counterparties began refusing to accept its trades and pulled repo funding. A classic Wall Street RUN -- but on an INVESTMENT bank, not a commercial bank. By Thursday March 13 the firm had only hours of cash left. T3: over the weekend of MARCH 15-16 2008, the Fed brokered an emergency sale to JPMORGAN CHASE at a price of $2 PER SHARE (later renegotiated to $10 after Bear shareholders threatened lawsuits). The Fed provided a $30 BILLION NON-RECOURSE LOAN through a special-purpose vehicle (Maiden Lane LLC) to take Bear's worst mortgage-backed assets off JPMorgan's books. T4: Bear stock had traded at $172 fourteen months earlier; the $2 sale price was a 99% loss for shareholders in a single weekend. But CREDITORS were paid 100 cents on the dollar -- including the counterparties whose panic had caused the run. The precedent: no investment bank would be allowed to just VANISH, but shareholders and executives would suffer. Critics from both the left (Nouriel Roubini, Paul Krugman) and the right (Peter Schiff, Marc Faber) warned that the rescue would encourage MORE risk-taking, not less. T5: this is textbook MORAL HAZARD in the sense economists mean it -- when a rescue institutionalizes the expectation of rescue, market discipline weakens and future risk-taking increases. The Bear precedent shaped the September 2008 expectation that Lehman would also be saved. When Lehman WAS NOT saved, the counterparty network priced-in exactly the outcome the Bear rescue had trained them not to expect. Further rungs: Jimmy Cayne, Bear's chairman, had been playing BRIDGE at a tournament during a critical week in July 2007 when the internal hedge funds collapsed -- the story became the anecdote of Wall Street executive detachment; the Maiden Lane LLC ultimately paid off, but this was invisible in real time.

name: Lehman Brothers: the day they let it fail
scope: The largest bankruptcy in US history and the Fed's decision NOT to rescue. T1: LEHMAN BROTHERS, founded 1850, was the FOURTH-LARGEST US investment bank in 2008 with $639 BILLION in assets. Its balance sheet was heavily exposed to mortgage-backed securities and commercial real estate. Its CEO was RICHARD FULD, who had run Lehman for 14 years and was known for aggressive expansion. T2: through the summer of 2008, Lehman's stock fell 80%. Attempts to sell the firm to Korea Development Bank (July) and Bank of America (early September) both failed. Over the weekend of SEPTEMBER 13-14 2008, Treasury Secretary HANK PAULSON and Fed Chair BEN BERNANKE gathered the heads of every major Wall Street bank at the New York Fed to try to arrange a private rescue. T3: unlike the March Bear rescue, Paulson and Bernanke ANNOUNCED they would NOT use taxpayer money to guarantee Lehman's assets for a buyer. Barclays, the most likely buyer, backed away when British regulators refused to bless the deal without a US backstop. On SUNDAY EVENING SEPTEMBER 14 2008, the private rescue talks collapsed. T4: at 1:45 AM on MONDAY SEPTEMBER 15 2008, Lehman filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy -- the LARGEST BANKRUPTCY IN AMERICAN HISTORY, with $639B in assets. The S&P 500 fell 4.7% that day; commercial paper markets froze; the Reserve Primary money-market fund 'broke the buck' the next day. T5: the decision to let Lehman fail is the MOST DEBATED single decision in modern Fed history. Paulson's memoir claims the Fed LACKED LEGAL AUTHORITY to lend to Lehman without adequate collateral. Bernanke's memoir says the same. Austrian critics (Peter Schiff, Bob Murphy) argue the failure PROVED the moral-hazard trap: markets had priced-in a rescue based on Bear, and the sudden removal of that expectation caused the panic. Others (Larry Ball's 2018 book 'The Fed and Lehman Brothers') argue the Fed HAD legal authority and chose not to use it. The counterfactual -- what happens if Lehman had been saved -- can never be tested. Further rungs: Fuld was reportedly worth roughly $500M when Lehman collapsed and lost most of it in the wipeout; Neil Barofsky (SIGTARP inspector general) later documented that the Fed had provided cheaper rescues to firms with worse balance sheets than Lehman.

name: AIG: the $182B backdoor bank rescue
scope: The insurance company whose rescue was really a rescue of the banks it had insured. T1: AMERICAN INTERNATIONAL GROUP (AIG), founded 1919, was one of the LARGEST INSURANCE companies in the world in 2008. Its London-based AIG FINANCIAL PRODUCTS unit had sold roughly $440 BILLION in CREDIT DEFAULT SWAPS (CDS) -- insurance contracts on mortgage-backed securities held by banks. T2: as the underlying MBS began defaulting through 2008, AIG's counterparties demanded COLLATERAL POSTINGS under the CDS contracts. AIG did not have the cash. On MONDAY SEPTEMBER 15 2008 -- the same day Lehman filed -- AIG faced billions in collateral calls and imminent collapse. T3: on TUESDAY SEPTEMBER 16 2008, the Federal Reserve announced an $85 BILLION emergency loan to AIG in exchange for 79.9% of the company. The loan grew over the following months to a total commitment of $182 BILLION -- the largest single bailout in US history. T4: the key point that took years to become visible: AIG's rescue was, in practical effect, a RESCUE OF ITS COUNTERPARTIES. AIG immediately used the loaned money to pay CDS collateral at 100 cents on the dollar to GOLDMAN SACHS ($12.9B), DEUTSCHE BANK ($11.8B), MERRILL LYNCH ($6.8B), SOCIETE GENERALE ($11.9B), BARCLAYS, UBS, and others (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact figures from SIGTARP reports). Every major dealer that had bought CDS protection from AIG was made whole -- through a NON-BANK conduit that avoided the political optics of a direct bank bailout. T5: this is the deepest Bastiat-pattern move of the entire 2008 rescue: the SEEN was 'saving AIG to prevent insurance-market collapse'; the UNSEEN was 'the money flowed straight through to Goldman, Deutsche, and the European megabanks.' It was a bank rescue laundered through an insurance company. Neil Barofsky's SIGTARP office made this visible in 2009-11 reports, at considerable political cost. Timothy Geithner (then NY Fed president) was the principal architect. Further rungs: AIG had been running unhedged CDS positions because its AAA credit rating had allowed it to sell insurance without posting collateral until downgraded; the US eventually recovered its full AIG loan with a small profit on paper by 2012 -- but the moral-hazard cost of the precedent is uncountable.

name: The Bank Term Funding Program: stealth QE at par

name: Richard Cantillon: the 1730s essay on money's first receivers
scope: The Irish-French economist whose 300-year-old insight explains the modern QE era. T1: RICHARD CANTILLON (c. 1680s-1734) was an IRISH-BORN banker who made a fortune in Paris financing John Law's Mississippi Company bubble and, crucially, SHORTED the bubble before it collapsed in 1720. T2: sometime in the 1730s he wrote in French a treatise titled 'ESSAI SUR LA NATURE DU COMMERCE EN GÉNÉRAL' ('Essay on the Nature of Trade in General'). He died in 1734 (his London townhouse burned mysteriously, in what may have been an insurance-fraud murder). The essay circulated in manuscript and was finally published in 1755, twenty-one years after his death. T3: Cantillon's KEY INSIGHT was that money creation is NOT NEUTRAL -- it does not raise all prices simultaneously. New money enters the economy at SPECIFIC POINTS (in his day, the mines that produced gold and silver, or the government-favored merchants who received the first coins); the FIRST-RECEIVERS get to spend the new money at OLD prices. Prices then rise as the money spreads, so LATE-RECEIVERS pay the higher prices with the old wages. The result is a REDISTRIBUTION from savers and wage-earners TO the first-receivers -- what modern Austrians call the CANTILLON EFFECT. T4: the modern QE-era application is direct. When the Fed creates reserves to buy Treasuries from primary dealers, the new money enters at the FED-DEALER interface. FIRST-RECEIVERS: banks, hedge funds, financial-sector employees, asset holders. LATE-RECEIVERS: wage-earners and savers who see consumer prices rise months or years later. The 2020-24 pattern (asset-price inflation in 2020-21 followed by consumer-price inflation in 2021-23) is textbook Cantillon-effect timing. T5: Cantillon's essay was cited by ADAM SMITH in 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), by JOHN STUART MILL, by CARL MENGER (the Austrian school's founder), and by MURRAY ROTHBARD who called Cantillon 'the founder of economic science.' The essay is a founding text of both classical and Austrian economics -- and its 300-year-old core insight explains why QE benefits Wall Street before it reaches Main Street. Further rungs: Cantillon originated the term 'entrepreneur' in its modern economic sense; his death by house fire remains unsolved.

name: MMT rise and fall: Stephanie Kelton's Deficit Myth
scope: The Modern Monetary Theory movement that peaked in 2020 and was falsified by 2022 inflation. T1: MODERN MONETARY THEORY (MMT) is a school of thought associated with economists WARREN MOSLER, L. RANDALL WRAY, and STEPHANIE KELTON. Its core claim: a country that issues its own FIAT CURRENCY faces NO SOLVENCY CONSTRAINT -- it can always create money to pay debts denominated in its own currency. T2: the movement moved from academic fringe to political prominence 2015-19 when Kelton, an economics professor at Stony Brook, served as CHIEF ECONOMIST for Bernie Sanders's Senate Budget Committee minority staff and advised the 2016 and 2020 Sanders presidential campaigns. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez publicly cited MMT as economic backing for the Green New Deal. T3: MMT's KEY FRAMING: 'The only real constraint on government spending is INFLATION and REAL RESOURCES, not political will or debt-service math.' Deficit financing is fine as long as excess capacity exists in the economy; taxes are for controlling inflation and redistributing resources, not for 'paying for' spending. Kelton's 2020 book 'THE DEFICIT MYTH: Modern Monetary Theory and the Birth of the People's Economy' reached the New York Times bestseller list. T4: the Austrian and monetarist critique -- from Larry White (George Mason), Bob Murphy (Mises Institute), Peter Schiff, Steve Hanke -- had been consistent: MMT is a repackaging of an old inflationist argument; there is no such thing as 'unused capacity' at aggregate scale that can absorb arbitrary monetary expansion without price adjustment; the constraint IS math, and it arrives via price adjustment rather than default. Larry Summers (a Democrat, but Old Keynesian rather than MMT) publicly called MMT 'the new voodoo economics' in a February 2019 Washington Post op-ed. T5: 2021-23 was the empirical test. The Biden administration's American Rescue Plan (MARCH 2021, $1.9T) was passed over Summers's specific published warning about inflation risk -- an MMT-adjacent bet that spending would not overheat prices. Inflation rose to a 9.1% CPI peak (June 2022). MMT proponents argued this was supply-chain-driven, not monetary. But the CORE MMT CLAIM (that the constraint on money-printing is real resources, not political will) was FALSIFIED by exactly the mechanism its critics had predicted -- prices adjusted to absorb the excess demand. By 2023-24 MMT as an intellectual movement had largely collapsed -- Kelton continued writing but the political prominence of 2019-21 was gone. Further rungs: Mosler's 1996 'Soft Currency Economics' is the movement's founding text; the term 'MMT' was popularized by Australian economist Bill Mitchell (University of Newcastle).

name: BRICS+ and the dollar-alternative movement
scope: The multi-country effort to build alternatives to the dollar-denominated global financial system. T1: BRICS is an intergovernmental grouping founded 2009 among BRAZIL, RUSSIA, INDIA, CHINA (the original four); SOUTH AFRICA was added in 2010, making the initial 'BRICS.' It is not a treaty organization but a coordination forum. T2: on JANUARY 1 2024, BRICS EXPANDED to add EGYPT, ETHIOPIA, IRAN, and the UNITED ARAB EMIRATES (Saudi Arabia was invited but delayed a decision; Argentina under Milei declined the December 2023 invitation from the previous Fernandez government). The expanded group is often called 'BRICS+' and represents roughly 45% of the global population and 35% of world GDP. T3: a KEY MOTIVATION for BRICS+ expansion has been growing frustration with DOLLAR-DENOMINATED international trade and the US Treasury's use of the SWIFT payment system for sanctions. After the FEBRUARY 2022 Russia invasion of Ukraine, the US and EU froze approximately $300 BILLION in Russian central bank reserves -- an unprecedented weaponization of the dollar system. This dramatically accelerated non-Western countries' interest in alternative payment rails. T4: SPECIFIC RESPONSES have emerged: (a) Russia-China bilateral trade shifted heavily to RUBLE-YUAN settlement post-2022 (Chinese customs data show over 90% of Russia-China trade now settled in local currencies); (b) India began paying for Russian oil in RUPEES and later UAE DIRHAMS; (c) Saudi Arabia signaled acceptance of yuan for some Chinese oil purchases (2023 Beijing summit); (d) BRICS discussion of a common trade-settlement instrument (sometimes called 'the BRICS currency' in press coverage, though no formal launch has occurred). T5: the movement does NOT threaten dollar HEGEMONY in the near term. The dollar remains roughly 58% of global FX reserves (down from 71% in 2000), 88% of foreign-exchange transactions have a dollar leg, and the US Treasury market has no serious alternative for global reserve holders. But the LONG-TERM directional trend is clear: the 2022 reserve-freeze precedent, combined with rising US debt-to-GDP (~120% in 2025), is driving diversification. Austrian analysts (Luke Gromen, Lyn Alden, Ammous) argue this is the beginning of a multi-decade re-weighting of global reserves toward NEUTRAL assets -- gold accumulation by central banks reached a 55-year high in 2022 and remained elevated through 2024. Further rungs: the term 'BRICS' was coined by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill in a 2001 paper; the acronym was originally 'BRIC' and became 'BRICS' when South Africa joined 2010.
